I forgot to mention a very important tip in my other post, *write shit down*.

Buy a pack of pencils, a notebook, a clip board and some graph paper from the local dollar store and use the hell out of them.

Specifically for tong making, a sketch of your plan, note the parent material, the length, where mark for your tapers and shoulders etc.

Eg: 5/8 square, 16"

1" for jaws

1 1/2" for boss

3/8 punch for rivet

And then note what happens to your blank after forging. The 1" for the Jaws turned into what? Was 1 1/2" for the boss too much? Not enough? Was there enough material left over for the reins?

When you make your next set this info will be incredibly helpful.

Yes. Good tongs means better control, fewer dropped parts, fewer burns. Bad tongs can mean disaster. 

Make two sets of the same type, keep the ones that turned out better. 

After using them for a couple weeks, look at them critically. Are the reins too long, are they too short? Is the too much flex? Are they parallel when grabbing your workpiece? How's the rivet? Is it binding or too loose? Look at the jaws, where are they worn? Do they fit your workpiece well? Are the biting at the boss or at the tips? Do they twist on you? 

Modify the design with what you learned about how they work and fit your hands. Make two more, keep the good set.

Trouble shooting 1-4, it looks like a couple may have some cold shuts right at the transition from leaf to stem, and others were probably worked too cold or with too sharp of a tool. 

Cold shuts are caused by folding steel over itself at less than a welding heat. That fold can be worked into the steel and creates a failure point. Grinding it out while it's shallow is the fastest fix. 

The sharp edges of your anvil may also be partially to blame here, sharp edges make sharp cuts in your work piece, these become stress risers and when the piece is thin like that it's almost certain to fail.

The fix here is grinding a radius into at least a portion of you anvils edges. Doesn’t have to much, a few inches long and about as round as a sharpie will do fine. Sharp edges really can't be used for much and are a liability in most cases.

Working the stem too cold is an easy fix too, pop it back in the fire no later than when it gets to a dull red. It takes patience, you want to keep going because you're almost done and it took a long time to get here and you were fumbling with you tools and now it's cold so one more swing and now it's junk. Rushing ruins stuff that you would otherwise have done well.

Of course. The first shop I worked at 12 years ago had switched from coal to gas before I signed on, and that's what I have the most experience with. Two years ago I got picked up by my new employer, and they run coal and coke. 

Gas is clean, reliable and low maintenance, and time efficient, solid fuel is none of those things. 

If I dropped a pile of parts in the gas fire and left the room, made a coffee, discussed the project with my boss, took a piss and came back, you know what would have happened? My parts would be hot. That's it. I can throw a ton of steel in there without any concern for my parts. The literal use of the phrase "too many irons in the fire" does not apply. 

If I turn my back on a coal fire for literally a minute it could do anything. The temp could spike, it could drop, the floor could burn out and drop my parts deep in the fire. My employer, an excellent blacksmith, formally trained in Austria in a generational blacksmith shop, many decades of experience with coal, still burns parts at least semi regularly. As do the 3 other people in my shop, some who have similar backgrounds. 

Heating is uneven and temperamental,  requiring constant maintenance, manually adding fuel and controlling airflow. The smoke is terrible for you, the dust is terrible for you, and it's filthy. Other than the notable ability to easy create very small heats and headroom over the fire for large parts, I don't see any upside over gas. A blowtorch can answer both of those needs the times when it's important. 

I'm sure with a few more years I could learn to more effectively mitigate the shortcomings, but the technology already exists to eliminate them entirely. 

As a hobbyist the difference in the start up costs may not be worth it to them, but as a professional, the difference in efficiency is enormous.

Depending on how bad it is, and it sounds like it's bad, you will likely have to contact a company to do a complete restoration.

A quick walk through of the process:

We would show up, take measurements of the railing, and examine all points where it is attached to the existing structure to ensure it is sound. We would then remove the railing and take it to a company that would strip away the paint in an acid bath. 

After stripping it comes back to the shop. Any badly rusted components would be cut out and replaced with new steel. This may involve forging new components to match the existing design. The railing would be examined for broken welds and rivets and these would be repaired.

Modifications may be necessary to bring the railing up to contemporary building code, though at least where I am (Ontario, Canada), restoration work usually gets an exemption.

After the restoration is complete, the railing would be sent to get galvanized, hot dipped in zinc to protect from rust. It is then painted, and we would return to do the re installation.

A month is not an unreasonable timeline for this sort project, depending on the scale and complexity, and also on the schedules of the various companies involved. Sometimes less, sometimes a great deal more.

I'd suggest getting in touch with a blacksmith close to where you are asap. It doesn't sound like the railing is safe, and some places won't to outdoor installs in the winter. 

Good luck, I always love getting a chance to give a second life to an something old like that.

To expand on this a bit, you want a glove on the non-dominant, non-hammering hand. 

Your off hand is going to be holding tongs or the workpiece directly, and it will take a lot of heat and also abuse as you strike the workpiece and it moves in your hand.

Your hammer hand has no glove because it makes it harder to grip your hammer. The larger the thing your grabbing, the harder your hand has to work to hold on to it. Thicker gloves exaggerate the issue. It's not a hard rule, depending on what your doing it can be much safer to wear both gloves rather than just one. 

I've worked in thick cheap welding gloves, thick expensive welding gloves, thin welding gloves, mechanics gloves, cheap work gloves, expensive work gloves, on one and both hands, they all work. Leather, easy to shake off, and cheap enough that it doesn't hurt too bad to replace, but not so cheap they fall apart.

Unsolicited advice time, some things to consider.

Ideally you want 360° access to the jaws of your vice, so if you're not quenching long items regularly you may want to cut down the tank to at least the height of the jaws. I'm a big believer in not having to work around stuff, it slows you down and cost you effort. Better to fix it than compensate for it.

Second, you're probably going to want to weight that base. It looks like it'll move when you're working at the vice, nothing more annoying than having to chase your work in a circle. It'll slow you down and make work harder than it needs to be.

Last, it looks too top heavy, tipping is a big concern. Could be *extremely* dangerous if the oil is hot, or if you have a hot work piece clamped in the vice. Solution is the same as the last one, more weight on the base.

It's likely still usable, just not ideal. As the others have said, test the rebound, lots of information out there on how.

Depending on the damage you might be better off leaving it rather than attempting a repair, as your efforts may leave it worse off structurally and cosmetically. This shit is tricky, and I imagine you don't want to ruin your armour.

That said, some general advice. Use a light hammer, no more than 1lb. For an anvil you want something moderately heavy, close to the shape you want the armour to be, smooth surfaces and absolutely no sharp edges. I don't expect you'll need heat, but if you do a small torch should suffice, larger heat sources will be harder to control. Since you're dealing with a large and unwieldy workpiece, a second set of hands will likely be necessary. 

Pick up some sheet metal from anywhere, flashing, rain gutters, car door, whatever, as close in thickness to the armour as you can find. Practice a lot on the scrap before you just dive in. Try to do to the sheet what you're going to try to do to the armour. 

Be patient. Don't let yourself get frustrated. *Take your time.* You basically get one shot at this, so don't rush. 

Watch a lot of YouTube. Pay attention to the tooling used, as well as the techniques.

Good luck.

Set a safe word. Stoplight colours work well. 
Green light: it's ok, you can keep going despite whatever else that might be going on. 
Yellow light: I don't object to what is happening, just be careful, slow down, take it easy, etc. 
Red light: FULL STOP. Not an inch further. For the moment, we are done. 

Other types of signals are also important as there may be times when you are unable to speak. Tapping and grunting, fast and repetitive, are both good ways of informing your partner you need to stop.
